summary: One of the three Baltic states, located in the middle. It first became independent in 1918, was annexed by the Soviet Union after World War II, and regained independence in 1991. The Art Nouveau architecture of the capital Riga is famous worldwide.

ranking.name: Lutheranism
ranking.description: During the 16th-century Reformation, the German nobility who ruled Latvia and cities such as Riga accepted Lutheranism, and Latvian peasants in the north and center converted with them. Lutheranism and German culture had a profound influence, and in 1689 the Bible was translated into Latvian. But the atheist policies of the Soviet period caused a large loss of believers, and today the proportion of Lutherans has fallen sharply.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: During 50 years of Soviet rule atheism was promoted, churches were closed and clergy persecuted, and many families stopped passing on religion. As a result Latvia has become one of the European countries with a higher proportion of people with no religion, concentrated mainly in cities such as Riga and in the younger generation.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodoxy was brought mainly by the Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians who moved in during the period of Russian imperial rule (18th–20th centuries) and the Soviet period, and believers are concentrated in Riga and cities in the east such as Daugavpils. After the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2022, the Latvian Orthodox Church declared its independence from the Moscow Patriarchate.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism is most common in Latgale in the southeast, because that region belonged to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1561 to 1772 and was not affected by the Lutheran Reformation. The Basilica of Aglona in Latgale is an important Catholic pilgrimage site and attracts large numbers of believers each August.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: These include the Old Believers (Russians who moved in in the 17th century to escape persecution over the Russian church reforms), Baptists, and the neopagan movement Dievturība (a Baltic traditional faith revived in the 20th century).

religion.background: The indigenous peoples of Latvia followed Baltic polytheism. In the 12th–13th centuries the German Teutonic Order and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword conquered the land in the "Northern Crusades", forced the local people to convert to Catholicism, and established the Livonian Order state. During the 16th-century Reformation, the German nobility and cities accepted Lutheranism, and Latvians in the north and center converted with them; the Latgale region in the southeast, after 1561, belonged to Poland–Lithuania and remained Catholic. From the 18th century the Russian Empire ruled the area, and Orthodoxy came with the Russians who moved in. During the Soviet period (1940–1991) atheism was promoted and large numbers of Russians moved in, so that today's religious map is divided into four major groups: Lutherans, Catholics, Orthodox and the non-religious.

ranking.name: Latvian
ranking.description: Latvian is the language of the Latvian nation. The 19th-century national awakening movement was centered on it, and it became the national language after independence in 1918. After independence was restored in 1991, the government established Latvian as the sole official language through the State Language Law (1999) and promoted a change in the language of school instruction to reverse the dominant position of Russian from the Soviet period.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russians moved in successively from the 18th century, but industrialization in the Soviet period (1940–1991) brought large numbers of Russian-speaking immigrants, so that ethnic Latvians for a time made up only a little more than half of the population. After 1991 many Soviet-period immigrants did not automatically obtain citizenship and became "non-citizens"; the issues of language and citizenship remain sensitive today. Russian is mainly used in Riga and the eastern cities.

language.history: Latvian belongs to the Baltic branch of the Indo-European language family and is close to Lithuanian. After the German knights' conquest in the 13th century, German became the language of the nobility and the cities, while Latvian was the language of the peasants. The first Latvian book (a Catholic catechism) was published in 1585, and in 1689 the Lutheran pastor Ernst Glück completed the translation of the Bible, laying the foundation of the written language. In the 19th century the "Young Latvians" movement promoted national awakening; after independence in 1918 Latvian became the national language. During the Soviet period large numbers of Russians moved in and Russian became the dominant language; after independence was restored in 1991 Latvian again became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Aukstā zupa (cold beet soup)
ranking.description: A pink cold soup made from pickled beets, cucumbers, dill and boiled eggs with fermented milk (kefir), eaten with hot potatoes.
ranking.history: Cold beet soup is a traditional summer dish of the Baltics and Eastern Europe, and the addition of fermented dairy products is a specialty of Latvia and Lithuania. In an era without refrigeration, fermented milk was a way of preserving milk, and in the heat of summer people drank the cold soup to cool off. Today it is the most common soup on Latvian family tables in summer.

ranking.name: Pīrāgi (bacon buns)
ranking.description: Half-moon-shaped small pies made from yeast dough filled with chopped bacon and onion and baked. The crust is soft and slightly sweet, the filling salty and savory, and they are a common festive treat.
ranking.history: The name pīrāgi shares its origin with the Russian pirozhki, reflecting the widespread pie tradition of Eastern Europe. The Latvian version, filled with bacon, comes from the tradition of farm families preserving meat after slaughtering pigs in winter. It is an indispensable treat at Christmas, Midsummer and all kinds of family celebrations, and is also the hometown food Latvian emigrants most often make abroad.

ranking.name: Sklandrausis (carrot and potato tart)
ranking.description: A sweet small tart with a rye pastry base, topped with mashed potato and mashed carrot and sprinkled with cinnamon before baking. It has a soft, sweet texture with the aroma of cinnamon and butter.
ranking.history: Sklandrausis originates in the Kurzeme region of western Latvia and is a traditional festive treat made from local products such as rye, potatoes and carrots. In 2013 it received the European Union's Traditional Specialities Guaranteed (TSG) certification, the first Latvian food to receive this certification, reflecting its important place in Latvian food culture.

ranking.name: Jāņu siers (Midsummer cheese)
ranking.description: A round fresh cheese made from milk, curds, eggs and caraway seeds, sliced and eaten with beer. It has a firm texture and the distinctive aroma of caraway.
ranking.history: Jāņu siers is a traditional food of Latvia's Midsummer festival (Jāņi, 23–24 June). Midsummer originates from the pre-Christian Baltic traditional faith celebrating the summer solstice; on this day people light bonfires, sing, wear flower wreaths, and eat caraway cheese with beer. The round cheese symbolizes the sun, and despite Christianization and the Soviet period, the customs of this festival have been fully preserved.

ranking.name: Rupjmaize (rye bread)
ranking.description: A dark, dense, slightly sour bread made from rye flour, sourdough starter and caraway seeds. It has a hearty texture with a sour taste and toasty aroma, and is often eaten with butter or smoked fish.
ranking.history: Rye is hardy and suited to Latvia's cold climate, and has been the main local grain since ancient times. Rye bread has sacred meaning in Latvian culture, and traditionally bread that fell was picked up and kissed. In the past farm families baked it weekly in large ovens at home to get through the long winter. Today rupjmaize remains the everyday staple of Latvians and an important cultural symbol.
